ideas.name: self-aligning flexure pad
ideas.description: A printed PLA pad (TPU face, friction 0.9) attached to the moving jaw's lower face by a thin TPU living hinge about 15 mm above the pad's contact centre. The hinge axis runs across the jaw, parallel to the hinge. The TPU web lets the pad rotate ±35° and springs it back to the stock angle when unloaded, so it does not flop during approach. Under squeeze, the contact force acts below the hinge, so the pad swings flat against the object's side. The fixed jaw gets a matching rigid TPU-faced pad with no reach. Overhang past the stock fingertip is 0–5 mm, so nothing new reaches over tall objects' tops.
ideas.test: Model the moving pad as a body on a revolute joint, with a torsional spring of about 0.05 N·m/rad and stops at ±35°, pivot 15 mm above the contact patch on the moving jaw. Rerun all 21 objects, checking the 73–96 mm group for face angle under squeeze and banana and potted meat for start-pose and descent contacts.

ideas.name: tie-rod levelled moving pad
ideas.description: The moving pad hangs on a 3 mm pin through an MR63 bearing at the stock jaw's fingertip. A printed tie rod, 81 mm long (the same as the jaw's hinge-to-tip radius), runs from a pin on a short arm above the pad to a fixed pin on the gripper body, offset from the jaw hinge by the same vector as the pad arm. Jaw, tie rod, body and pad arm form a parallelogram, so the pad face stays parallel to the fixed face from 17 to 96 mm. The servo still drives the jaw, so the squeeze stays 20 N. The face keeps a 1 mm TPU skin (friction 0.9), the shoe has 8 mm of reach, and the pad arm and tie rod sit behind the jaw so they clear the fixed pad when closed.
ideas.test: A pads-slot builder that mounts a pivoting pad at the revolute fingertip with its orientation constrained by a tie rod to the frame (a four-bar). It needs interference checks over the jaw's -0.17 to 1.20 rad, mostly the tie rod against the wrist and the fixed pad near closed.

ideas.name: bridged long slide with rack preload roller
ideas.description: This replaces the stock revolute moving jaw. A printed bridge frame on the gripper body clamps two 3 x 150 mm ground steel rods at both ends, so the rods are simply supported and never cantilevered. A printed carriage rides the rods on four LM3UU bushings, two per rod and spaced about 30 mm apart, to resist the moment from the squeeze. A printed module-1 rack on the carriage meshes with a printed 55 mm pitch-radius gear sector on the gripper servo horn. The sector has teeth only over the roughly 110 deg arc in mesh, so it clears the arm. A small idler on two MR63 bearings, carried by the frame on an M3 shaft, rolls on the back of the rack and preloads it into the sector, so the squeeze cannot lift the rack and skip teeth. The moving finger hangs from the carriage with its face vertical and slides straight along the closing axis. It neither turns nor rises, and it travels about 55 mm per servo radian: about 106 mm over the -0.17..1.75 rad range, so the fingertips open from about 0 to 100 mm. The squeeze is about 29 N (1.62 N*m / 0.055 m). The fixed jaw and the existing pads, re-angled to 0 deg, are reused.
ideas.test: A jaw builder for a prismatic finger whose rods are supported at both ends. It would take four bushings at a set spacing (the per-bushing load from squeeze and moment against the 52.9 N rating), a back-of-rack preload roller (rack separation held at 0 mm, so no skip check failure), and a sector of radius 50–60 mm with an opening offset so that -0.17 rad gives about 0 mm and 1.75 rad gives about 100 mm. Trial it with pads at pad_angle 0, then check the closing face for interference at full close.

ideas.name: kinked moving pad (two-angle toe)
ideas.description: A printed moving pad whose face has two planar facets. The upper facet keeps the current 31 deg pre-tilt. The lower 14 mm toe is tilted a further 12 deg bottom-in, and the whole face is moved back 3 mm so the toe tip stays at today's tip position. At wide openings, where the hinge has raised the tip 22-28 mm, only the toe reaches below a low box's top, and it is near-vertical (+15 deg at 85 mm, about +1 deg at 75 mm) rather than +27 deg. At small openings, objects meet either the unchanged tip (flat-sided objects) or the unchanged 31 deg upper face at their equator (round objects). TPU skin 3 mm on both facets, width 9.05 mm, reach 8 mm, fixed pad unchanged. Same 4 x M2 mounting.
ideas.test: Extend design/fingers.py with toe_angle_deg [0,20] and toe_height_mm [0,20] on the moving pad (face recessed so the toe tip is invariant). Run the interference check over -0.17..1.20 rad, then trial pudding_box, sugar_box, tuna_fish_can, and as held-group guards large_marker, banana, golf_ball, strawberry, dice and potted_meat_can.

ideas.name: opening-triggered drop toe on the moving pad
ideas.description: A printed toe (about 9 mm wide, 30 mm long, with a 1 mm TPU skin) rides in a dovetail slide cut into the back of the moving pad. The slide's axis is set about 30° to the pad face, so it points straight down when the jaw is at about 1.05 rad. The toe's contact face is printed at the same 30°, so it is vertical at 1.05 rad and within about ±6° of vertical over 0.95–1.15 rad (85–96 mm). A short printed pushrod connects a pin on the toe to a pin on the fixed gripper body, offset about 12 mm from the hinge axis. The pushrod end has a slot about 0.9 rad of jaw travel long (lost motion). Below about 0.9 rad (openings ≤77 mm) the pin floats in the slot, and a printed detent holds the toe flush inside the pad, so the hand is unchanged for every held object. Above 0.9 rad, the growing distance between the body pin and the jaw pulls the toe down its slide. Near toggle this gives about 12 mm of drop at 1.0 rad, 20 mm at 1.07 and 28 mm at 1.15. That cancels the brief's +22 mm (85 mm) and +28 to +33 mm (91–95 mm) tip rise, so the moving contact lands 5–15 mm below the tops of tuna (+17), pudding (+19), sugar (+23) and mustard (+29). The pushrod sets the toe's position kinematically, so the object's weight is carried in the slide and link rather than by friction. Squeeze at the toe is about 20 N × 89/110 ≈ 16 N, giving 2·0.5·16 = 16 N of grip against the sugar box's 5.0 N.
ideas.slot: moving_toe (on the moving pad; pads stay at pad_angle 30.972, reach 8, TPU 3, width 9.05)
ideas.test: The simulator needs a builder for a jaw-mounted prismatic sub-part whose extension is a set function of jaw angle: e(q) = 0 for q < 0.9 rad, then the slider-crank curve above, with the toe face tilted 30° in the jaw frame. It also needs collision geometry for the toe, the pushrod and the body bracket, swept over the whole −0.17..1.20 rad range for the no-interference law. Then rerun the 4 failing groups and all 17 held groups. Apple, gelatin and tomato soup are the ones to watch near the 0.9 rad threshold.

ideas.name: convex rocker moving pad (cylindrical crowned face)
ideas.description: The flat moving pad is replaced by a printed pad whose gripping face is a circular arc in the closing plane: radius about 20 mm, axis parallel to the hinge, spanning ±35 deg, with the arc centre at the current fingertip height (reach 8). It has a 3 mm TPU skin, friction 0.9. As the revolute jaw turns from 0.21 rad (17 mm) to 1.18 rad (95 mm), the face's tilt runs from −19 to +37 deg. Somewhere on the arc there is always a point whose normal is horizontal, and that point meets a vertical box side, so the grip stays antipodal to the vertical fixed face. The fixed pad stays flat. Squeeze is unchanged at 20 N, since the lever is still about 81 + 8 mm.

proposals.edit: pads -> pads (groove_mm=2, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=45, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=15, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (8 of 9 failing tasks) and squeezed_down_out (gelatin box). The hinged jaw pivots 81 mm above its fingertip, so the fingertip rises as the jaw opens and the face tilts. The brief gives +14 mm / 44 deg at 75 mm, +23 mm / 53 deg at 85 mm and +35 mm / 64 deg at 95 mm. On these low, wide objects that puts the tip above the object's half-height: tuna can tip +23 to +27 vs top +17, pudding box +17 to +19 vs +19, sugar box +22 to +23 vs +23, mustard bottle +14 vs +29 but with the face 66 to 84 deg 'pushing down'. So the moving jaw presses on the top face (55 to 84 deg down) and never makes an opposed contact. On the gelatin box (73 mm) the jaw does reach the side, but the face is tilted 33 deg, so N sin33 = 0.54 N pushes the box down, more than the mu = 0.5 friction can hold, and the box is squeezed out.
proposals.principle: A face that turns with its joint is parallel to the fixed face at one opening only. Tilting the moving pad back by pad_angle moves that parallel opening out to the wide objects, and it also points the pad's extension closer to vertical at wide openings, which lowers the tip. A tilted contact holds when tan(a) < mu, so a TPU skin (mu 0.9 instead of 0.45) tolerates the remaining tilt. Squeeze is unchanged at 20 N: 2 x 0.9 x 20 = 36 N against 5 N for the 514 g sugar box.
proposals.hypothesis: Brief, pads at pad_angle 45: 85 mm gives face +14 deg (was +53) and tip +14 mm (was +23); 55 mm gives -8 deg, -5 mm. Interpolating, 73 mm is about +5 deg / +8 mm, under the gelatin box's +15 top. 90 mm is about +19 deg / +17 mm, around the pudding box's +19. 92 mm is about +21 deg / +19 mm, under the sugar box's +23. 96 mm is about +25 deg / +21 mm, under the mustard bottle's +29. tan(25 deg) = 0.47, below TPU's 0.9, so the residual tilt holds. The tuna can (tip +14 vs top +17) is the tightest case. No params move on the current body changes the hinge geometry, so a params move cannot fix this. The parallelogram makes the rise worse (+33 mm at 85 mm with link 90). Prismatic reaches only 68 mm. long_slide at sector 50 skips teeth at 85 mm (rack lifts 2.2 mm, the limit is 0.5) and overloads its bushings at every width (138 N vs 52.9 rated). Pads are the only catalogue part that changes the tip and face at wide openings, and they cost $0, 0 days and 18 machine minutes.
risks: Small objects (dice 17 mm, large_marker 19, wood_block_cube 26, flat_screwdriver 34, golf_ball 42): at 35 mm the moving face is now -21 deg with its tip 10 mm below the fixed one. That pushes the object up and needs table clearance. They should survive because tan(21 deg) = 0.38 < 0.9 with TPU, and System 1 can raise grasp.depth to clear the table. The dice is the worst case: at 17 tall it leaves the least room for a lower tip.

Round held objects (golf_ball, plum, strawberry, lemon, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple): the face tilt changes at every opening. The 2 mm V-groove centres spheres, and most of them (55 to 75 mm) move closer to parallel than they were on the stock jaw.
Heavy cans (potted_meat_can, tomato_soup_can, mu 0.35): TPU raises the friction to 0.9, so they gain margin.

proposals.mechanism: Same mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face and squeezed_down_out, caused by the hinged jaw's fingertip rising (+23 mm at 85 mm) and its face tilting (53 deg) at wide openings.
proposals.principle: Fingertip rise scales with how the finger's extension is oriented relative to vertical. A longer pad tilted back 45 deg points almost straight down at wide openings (jaw near 50 deg), so its extra length lowers the moving tip almost as much as the fixed pad's. A thicker TPU skin (mu 0.9) holds the leftover tilt and conforms to the cardboard corners.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the alternative point in the pads range: full reach (30 mm), maximum TPU, and no groove, so the flat cardboard and metal faces get a full flat contact patch. If proposal 1 leaves the tuna can or pudding box marginal (tip about 2 to 3 mm under the top), the extra reach gives fingers that reach lower on the box sides while the jaw is wide open. I am offering it as a second, separately tried value in case 15 mm of reach does not clear the tuna can. Like proposal 1 it is free and takes 18 machine minutes. The catalogue swaps that cost money are ruled out by the brief's own numbers, as shown in proposal 1.
risks: dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube: longer pads make the fingertips sit lower, and a moving tip below the fixed one at small openings needs more table clearance. System 1 can re-tune grasp.depth to recover it.
Rolling held objects (golf_ball, plum, strawberry): with no groove these spheres are not centred, so they rely on TPU friction alone. That is the reason proposal 1 keeps a 2 mm groove.

The diagnosis is the same for all 5 failing groups. They are low and wide (73 to 96 mm across, 30 to 58 mm tall). At those openings the stock hinged jaw's fingertip rises 14 to 27 mm and its face tilts 33 to 84 deg, so the moving jaw lands on the top face or pushes the box down and out.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face: on the hinged stock jaw the moving fingertip rises as the jaw opens (+17 mm at 78 mm, +23 mm at 85 mm, +27 mm at 89 mm) and ends up above the top of the low wide objects (gelatin top +15, tuna +17, pudding +19, sugar +23), so it presses 55-84 deg down on the top face. Where it does reach the side, the face is 33 deg off parallel and squeezes the box down and out.
proposals.principle: A finger holds a side only if, at that object's opening, its tip reaches below the object's top. Tilting the moving pad back by pad_angle makes its face parallel at a wide opening and lowers its tip there. A TPU skin (mu 0.9, so it holds up to atan 0.9 = 42 deg) holds the remaining tilt. Reach controls how far the tilted pad tip sticks inward, and in iteration 1 that inward tip landed on the tops of the tall mid-size objects.
proposals.hypothesis: In iteration 1, pads at angle 45 with reach 30 gained all 5 failing groups. They lost apple, banana, cup, potted_meat_can, tennis_ball and tomato_soup_can to force_limit: a pad pressed 46 N down on the potted meat can's top at +40 mm (top +42) during the descent. A 45-deg pad extended 30 mm tilts inward and lands on a tall object's top. The tuning trials only moved reach to 29.5, so short reach was never tested. Brief at pad_angle 45 (mid reach): 85 mm gives face +14 deg, tip +14 mm (under tuna +17); interpolating, about +7 mm at 73 mm (gelatin +15), about +19 mm at 92 mm (sugar +23) and about +22 mm at 96 mm (mustard +29). The tilt is under 25 deg, so TPU holds it. Halving reach to 15 roughly halves the inward hook that hit the tall objects. Cheaper moves won't do: params on the bare stock jaw can't stop the hinge rise, and the slides fail their own limits (long_slide at 50 mm: rack lifts 2.2 mm, bushings loaded 138 N against a 52.9 N rating).
risks: potted_meat_can, cup, apple, tennis_ball, tomato_soup_can, banana: reach 30 hooked the tilted pad onto their tops. Reach 15 halves that overhang, so it should clear, but it's the main risk.

dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube: near closed the moving face sits about -21 deg or more (bottom in). They held under the same angle in iteration 1, and TPU at mu 0.9 covers it. The closed-jaw interference refusal could come back; groove 0 is meant to prevent it.

iterations.notes:
I've proposed three pad bodies. Each is free: $0, no lead time, 18 machine minutes, using m2 screws already on hand plus about 2 g PLA and 1 g TPU. I'm not buying anything this round.

Why pads and not another part:
- **12 V servos:** refused, because they cost $68 against the $40 left.
- **Prismatic slide:** opens only 68 mm, too narrow for the 73-96 mm objects.
- **Parallelogram jaw (90 mm links):** the tip rises more, +33 mm at 85 mm against +23 mm on the stock jaw.
- **Long slide (50 mm sector):** fails its own limits. The rack lifts 2.2 mm off the gear at 85 mm (teeth skip past 0.5 mm), and each bushing carries 138 N against a 52.9 N rating.

What iteration 1 showed: pads tilted 45 deg with 30 mm reach did gain all 5 failing groups. But they lost 6 held ones: apple, banana, cup, potted meat can, tennis ball and tomato soup can. The potted meat can log shows a pad pressing 46 N down on its top during the descent. The follow-up trials only moved reach to 29.5 mm, so a short reach was never tested.

The three proposals all use the pads part with groove 0 and a 3 mm TPU skin:
1. **45 deg tilt, 15 mm reach:** halves the overhang that landed on the tall objects.
2. **45 deg tilt, 20 mm reach:** more tip depth for the two closest cases, the pudding box and tuna can.
3. **38 deg tilt, 22 mm reach:** less tilt, in case the 45 deg angle itself caused the collisions.

I set groove to 0 because the refused reach-15 proposal had a 2 mm groove. I think the groove's extra pad thickness caused the 0.3 mm overlap between the pads at the closed jaw, but that is a guess, so the same refusal could come back. If none of these holds every held group without colliding, the next step is to keep the 45 deg tilt and test reach between 8 and 30 mm. proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1−cos q), and its face is parallel to the fixed face at one opening only. A finger that slides straight along the closing axis neither rises nor turns, so its face stays vertical and opposite the fixed face at every width.

proposals.edit: jaw -> parallelogram (link_mm=90)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face, which shows up as squeezed_down_out on the gelatin box. The hinged moving face is tilted 44–64 deg (bottom swung out) at the openings the wide objects need: 73 mm ≈ 42 deg, 85 mm = 53 deg, 92–96 mm ≈ 60–64 deg. Because the upper face leans in, the face meets the object's top edge first and pushes 55–84 deg down (for example 29 N at 84 deg down on the pudding box, 30 N at 79 deg on the sugar box). Fingertip rise is the smaller factor: on the tuna can the moving tip is +27 mm against a +17 mm top, but the fixed tip sits about 15 mm below centre, so the moving tip is still below the top. The tilted face is what lands on the top.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel to the fixed face at one opening only. A four-bar carries the finger without turning it, so its face stays parallel at every opening.
proposals.hypothesis: Parallelogram with link_mm=90. The brief gives the face at -0 deg at 35, 55 and 85 mm, fingertips up to 106 mm apart (enough for the 96 mm mustard bottle) and a squeeze of 18–28 N, about the stock 20 N. With vertical faces every contact normal is horizontal, which removes the 'pushing 33–84 deg down' mechanism. The fingertip still rises on its circle: +9 mm at 55, +33 mm at 85, about +20 mm at 73 and about +40 mm at 92. Taking the fixed tip as about 3 mm above the table: on the gelatin box (top +15) the moving tip lands near +7, inside the side, so it is a clear gain. Sugar box: tip about +20 against a +22 top, marginal. Mustard bottle: about +19 against +29, a contact on the bottle's rounded upper side, possible. Tuna can (+18 against +17) and pudding box (about +21 against +19) will probably still catch the top edge, but on a vertical face rather than a 53–60 deg one, so the push is mostly horizontal. Why not cheaper moves: no stock-hinge parameter changes face tilt against opening (System 1 has already tuned the grasp, 9 attempts each). Every hinge+pads variant gained the five groups but lost banana and potted_meat_can across reach 15–30, angle 38–45 and width 8–17. The slides are refused at sector 50 (wrist interference). They also skip teeth at wide openings (rack lifts 2.2 mm at 85 mm, 0.5 mm limit) and overload the bushings (138–260 N on a 52.9 N rating), so they fail on exactly the objects we need. The 12 V servos cost $68 against $40 left and do not address the mechanism. Cost: 4 mr63 bearings at $0.90 = $3.60, 3 days, 16 g PLA = 82 machine min; the M3 screws are on hand.
risks: Rolling objects (apple 75 mm, tennis_ball 66, tomato_soup_can 68 lying): the moving tip rises about +14 to +25 mm at these openings. The equators sit 33–36 mm above the table, so both contacts stay below them on vertical faces and should survive. That is better than the current 36–44 deg tilted faces, which are what push these objects down.
potted_meat_can (370 g, mu 0.35): squeeze at 55–57 mm is 20 N, the same as stock, so 2·0.35·20 = 14 N against 3.6 N of weight. It survives.
dice / large_marker (17–19 mm): the servo range -0.17..1.55 rad covers closing, but the closed geometry is new. If the four-bar cannot close fully, the smallest objects are at risk.

idea.name: bridged long slide with rack preload roller
idea.description: This replaces the stock revolute moving jaw. A printed bridge frame on the gripper body clamps two 3 x 150 mm ground steel rods at both ends, so the rods are simply supported and never cantilevered. A printed carriage rides the rods on four LM3UU bushings, two per rod and spaced about 30 mm apart, to resist the moment from the squeeze. A printed module-1 rack on the carriage meshes with a printed 55 mm pitch-radius gear sector on the gripper servo horn. The sector has teeth only over the roughly 110 deg arc in mesh, so it clears the arm. A small idler on two MR63 bearings, carried by the frame on an M3 shaft, rolls on the back of the rack and preloads it into the sector, so the squeeze cannot lift the rack and skip teeth. The moving finger hangs from the carriage with its face vertical and slides straight along the closing axis. It neither turns nor rises, and it travels about 55 mm per servo radian: about 106 mm over the -0.17..1.75 rad range, so the fingertips open from about 0 to 100 mm. The squeeze is about 29 N (1.62 N*m / 0.055 m). The fixed jaw and the existing pads, re-angled to 0 deg, are reused.

Its bottom edge rides onto the box top and pushes 62–84 deg down, often with no fixed-jaw contact at all.

- **The trade-off:** banana is gripped near a 38 mm local opening and the boxes at 85–96 mm. Over that span the servo turns from about 0.45 to 1.18 rad, so the face rotates about 40 deg. Pad angles of 35–37.5 gained nothing and lost banana. Angles of 38 and up gained the wide groups and also lost banana.

- **Parallelogram:** reaches 91 mm at most, its tip rises 64 mm, and it lost 8 groups.

- the rods are clamped at both ends, not held from one end;
- the carriage runs on four bushings instead of two;
- a preload roller behind the rack keeps it meshed with the gear;
- a larger 55 mm gear gives about 0–100 mm of opening and about 29 N of squeeze, with a vertical face that doesn't rise.

idea.name: opening-triggered drop toe on the moving pad
idea.description: A printed toe (about 9 mm wide, 30 mm long, with a 1 mm TPU skin) rides in a dovetail slide cut into the back of the moving pad. The slide's axis is set about 30° to the pad face, so it points straight down when the jaw is at about 1.05 rad. The toe's contact face is printed at the same 30°, so it is vertical at 1.05 rad and within about ±6° of vertical over 0.95–1.15 rad (85–96 mm). A short printed pushrod connects a pin on the toe to a pin on the fixed gripper body, offset about 12 mm from the hinge axis. The pushrod end has a slot about 0.9 rad of jaw travel long (lost motion). Below about 0.9 rad (openings ≤77 mm) the pin floats in the slot, and a printed detent holds the toe flush inside the pad, so the hand is unchanged for every held object. Above 0.9 rad, the growing distance between the body pin and the jaw pulls the toe down its slide. Near toggle this gives about 12 mm of drop at 1.0 rad, 20 mm at 1.07 and 28 mm at 1.15. That cancels the brief's +22 mm (85 mm) and +28 to +33 mm (91–95 mm) tip rise, so the moving contact lands 5–15 mm below the tops of tuna (+17), pudding (+19), sugar (+23) and mustard (+29). The pushrod sets the toe's position kinematically, so the object's weight is carried in the slide and link rather than by friction. Squeeze at the toe is about 20 N × 89/110 ≈ 16 N, giving 2·0.5·16 = 16 N of grip against the sugar box's 5.0 N.

On the revolute jaw the flat moving pad is parallel to the fixed face at one opening only, about 45 mm with pad_angle 30.97. Its upper edge then lands on the box's top edge and pushes 62–84 deg downward (pudding 1–18 N, sugar 20–23 N, mustard 22 N). The fixed jaw gets little or no contact.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A flat face turning with its joint meets that condition at one opening only. A convex cylindrical face (axis parallel to the hinge) has a point whose normal is horizontal at every jaw angle inside its arc, so it stays antipodal to the vertical fixed face across the whole opening range. The contact just slides along the arc as the jaw turns.
proposals.hypothesis: The record shows no flat pad angle serves both ends of the opening range. Pudding, sugar and tuna need angle ≥38 (b041 at 40: face about +19 deg at 85 mm). Banana's middle is gripped near a 38 mm local opening and is lost at every angle ≥35, where the face at 38 mm tilts −10 deg or more with the bottom swung in. Reach ≥10 loses potted meat (top pressed 26–45 N). Lips and thin TPU were refused for interference. The jaw swaps fail on the brief's numbers: the parallelogram's tip rises +64 mm at 85 mm, the prismatic opens only 53 mm, and the long slide opens 88 mm with its teeth skipping 3.7 mm. Unlike the recorded flat or two-facet pads, a convex rocker face makes the normal horizontal at any opening from 17 to 96 mm. The contact sits at the height of the arc's centre, which we place at the fingertip. At 85–91 mm the moving tip is +22 to +28 mm, so on a box resting on the table the contact sits about 25 mm up. That is below the tops of pudding (38 mm), sugar (45 mm) and tuna (34 mm), so the squeeze becomes a side grip instead of a push on the top edge. On the mustard bottle the normal still runs through the bottle's axis, about 12 deg down, which friction 0.4 can hold (tan 12° = 0.21). It is a rigid printed part on the existing m2 screws, so it costs no money and no lead time.
risks: Round objects (golf_ball, plum, lemon, strawberry, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple, tomato_soup_can): a convex face against a sphere gives a point contact with less centring than today's flat tilted face, so they may roll out. dice, wood_block_cube, large_marker: at 17–26 mm the arc's lower part could touch the table, so the arc must stay within the 8 mm reach envelope.
potted_meat_can: the arc must not add effective reach, because reach ≥10 is what pressed its top.

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=0, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=33.5, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=8, width_mm=9.05)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding_box, sugar_box, mustard_bottle), plus fixed_jaw_missed on tuna_fish_can: at the 82-90 mm openings reached, the moving fingertip sits +18 to +25 mm above the fixed one, so it lands on the top face (63-84 deg down) instead of the side.
proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises as the jaw opens, and a finger can only hold a side if its tip reaches below the object's top at that object's opening. Thinner pads reach a given object width at a smaller servo angle, which lowers the tip.
proposals.hypothesis:
Thin the TPU from 3 to 2 mm and lower the angle from 34.2 to 33.5 deg. This lever has not been trialled below 2.68 mm TPU. It separates the wide-object tip height from banana's face tilt, which pad angle alone cannot do.

Effect of the thinner TPU: 1 mm less per face adds 2 mm of opening at the same servo angle. From the brief's table, that lowers the servo angle at a given width by about 0.022 rad at mid-range and 0.03 rad at the wide end. The tip slope at the wide end is 0.8-1.1 mm per mm of width (+12, +20, +31 mm at 75, 85, 95 mm), so the tip drops about 2 mm. Maximum opening also grows from 96 to about 98 mm, which gives more room around the 90-96 mm objects.

Effect on banana: the servo shift tilts the mid-range face about 1.2 deg, or about 1.3 deg of pad angle at the brief's 0.91 deg per deg. Angle 33.5 with 2 mm TPU therefore gives banana's opening about the tilt of angle 34.8 at 3 mm. 34.8 held every group and 35.4 lost banana, so this sits at the edge of the known-safe band.

Net at the wide end: tip about 1.8 mm lower (lowering the angle by 0.7 deg gives back about 0.2 mm at 0.29 mm/deg), face about 1 deg closer to parallel. The iteration 13 estimate put reg_pudding about 2 mm of contact height short, so this is the right size for pudding. These are interpolations from the brief, not simulated values.

Cheaper or other moves will not do: angle alone is capped by banana between 34.8 and 35.4. Reach barely changes the moving tip relative to the fixed one, and reach 10 lost potted meat in its only recent trial. Lips were refused for interference. Swaps fail on the brief's numbers: long_slide at sector 50 has rack lift of 3.7 mm against a 0.5 mm skip limit and bushings at 138 N against 52.9 N rated, parallelogram at link 90 has its tip at +65 mm at 85 mm, and prismatic opens only to 53 mm. servos_12v is refused ($68 against $40 left) and does not address this mechanism.
risks: banana: the mid-range tilt is about equal to angle 34.8, the highest value known to hold it. If thickness affects banana beyond tilt, it could still hit the force limit seen at 35.4. Thinner pads should also add clearance at the start pose.
No-interference refusal: TPU 1 mm was refused over a 0.2 x 1.3 x 0.1 mm overlap at jaw -0.16 rad. Stopping at 2 mm should clear it, but this is not proven.
potted_meat_can: should survive, since reach stays at 8 mm and the opening grows slightly.

dice, large_marker and wood_block_cube: their faces are already 16-21 deg swung in and tilt about 0.7 deg more net. Friction 0.9 and the 20 N squeeze are unchanged, assuming thin TPU keeps friction 0.9, and all three are very light (5-16 g).

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=0, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=32.7, pad_tpu_mm=1.5, reach_mm=8, width_mm=9.05)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on the wide low objects (pudding_box, sugar_box), where the moving fingertip rides too high at the object's opening.
proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises with opening, so reaching a given width at a smaller servo angle puts the tip below the object's top. Each face's thickness sets that servo angle.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the stronger version of the same lever: TPU 1.5 mm at angle 32.7 deg. Thinning by 1.5 mm per face adds 3 mm of opening, so maximum opening is about 99 mm. That lowers the tip about 3 mm at the wide end, and the lower angle gives back about 0.4 mm, for a net of about 2.6 mm. It tilts the mid-range face about 1.8 deg, or about 2 deg of pad angle, so banana sees about the tilt of 34.7 at 3 mm, inside the band that held. The wide-end face improves by only about 1 deg, so a sugar_box gain depends on tip height and opening mattering more than face tilt. Earlier gains at angles of 38 and up came with about 4 deg or more of face change, so sugar is a stretch. Mustard at 96 mm is unlikely, and I do not predict it.
risks: No-interference refusal: this is nearer the TPU 1 mm refusal, whose overlap was only 0.1 mm deep at jaw -0.16 rad. Clearance at 1.5 mm is unproven. A refusal costs no held group.
banana: same tilt reasoning as the first proposal, but the thickness extrapolation is larger, so confidence is lower.

Angle 32.7 is below the lowest lip-free value in the visible record (33.5). Lip trials at 31 and 33 deg were refused for pad-on-pad overlap, which I attribute mainly to the lip. Thinner faces should reduce this overlap, but that is untested.
Small objects (dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube): tilt is about unchanged from angle 34.7, which should keep them. This assumes friction 0.9 holds at 1.5 mm TPU.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on reg_pudding_box and fixed_jaw_missed on rva000_tuna_fish_can, the two failing groups closest to passing, since their other placements already pass.
proposals.principle: A face that turns with its joint is parallel at one opening only. Thinning the pad and lowering its angle together keep the face tilt at a mid-range opening while lowering the tip at wide openings.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the banana-safe hedge: TPU 2 mm at angle 32.9 deg. It cancels the mid-range tilt shift almost exactly (about 1.2 deg from the servo shift, against 1.3 deg of angle at 0.91 deg per deg). Banana's face should then stay at about today's tilt, not at the 34.8-equivalent edge used in the first proposal. It keeps most of the wide-end benefit: tip about 1.6 mm lower (about 2 mm from thinning, less 0.4 mm from the angle) and about 2 mm more opening, with the wide-end face about unchanged. If the first proposal loses banana, this one separates tilt from thickness as the cause. Its gain is less certain, because it has about 0.2 mm less tip drop and about 0.6 deg less face correction than the first proposal, so it may fall short of the roughly 2 mm pudding needs.
risks: banana: lowest risk of the three, since mid-range tilt is about unchanged. The remaining risk is any effect of thickness itself.
No-interference refusal: TPU 2 mm should clear the overlap seen at 1 mm, and thinner faces should not add pad-on-pad overlap, but angle 32.9 without a lip is untested.

Potted_meat_can, cup and the wide held objects (apple, gelatin_box, tomato_soup_can): should survive, since the tip is lower and the opening larger at unchanged reach. System 1 may need to re-tune grasp.side because the fixed face also moves back 1 mm.

iterations.notes:
All three proposals test one lever: TPU thickness, combined with a compensating drop in pad angle. Its only recorded test below 2.68 mm was TPU 1 mm, which was refused before trial over a 0.1 mm deep overlap, so 1.5-2 mm has never been tried.

The numbers are my interpolations from the brief's tables, not simulator output. I assume TPU keeps friction 0.9 at any thickness, as the catalogue implies, and that banana's limit depends mainly on face tilt. The record supports that second assumption only indirectly.

Expect a partial result at best. Pudding and tuna are realistic gains, sugar is a stretch, and I do not predict mustard: at 96 mm it is at the jaw's limit, and the record shows it gained only at angle 45 with reach 15-20. Recent pads parameter moves have gained tasks but no whole groups, so a zero-group result would not be surprising.

Cost is about 16-18 machine min per pad print, which is my estimate, with $0 spent, since the material comes from the printer and the screws are reused.
